newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germans detain man, son in millionaire's abduction.
newsitem.headline: Germans detain man, son in millionaire's abduction.

text.p: A judge on Thursday ordered a German man and his son detained on suspicion they helped kidnap a Frankfurt multi-millionaire, target of a massive police search for more than two weeks.
A Frankfurt judge ordered Rainer Koerppen, 48, held in a local jail as police stepped up investigation into the disappearance of businessman Jakub Fiszman by searching rural areas near Frankfurt.
Koerppen's 26-year-old son from his first marriage was also ordered held in custody, prosecutors said.
Fiszman, who comes from a prominent Jewish family in Poland, was abducted late at night outside his Frankfurt area office.

Police said they still hoped Fiszman, a 40-year-old best known for financing the failed Frankfurt production of the rock musical "Tommy," was alive and may be locked alone in a cellar or buried in a concealed dungeon.

Frankfurt prosecutors' office spokesman Rainer Schilling said in a German television interview about Koerppen: "This is a man with a long and violent criminal history who we believe to be one of the main suspects in this kidnapping case."

About 500 police on Thursday armed with machetes and sniffer dogs combed a densly-wooded and steep area in the Taunus region about 50 km (30 miles) west of Frankfurt in search of Fiszman, whom police say they hope is still alive.
Since October 1, the only word from Fiszman, who needs medication for severe food allergies, has been a telephone call to a friend he made the day after his abduction.

Prosecutors on Thursday also released two other suspects who had been held with Koerppen and his family since being arrested on Wednesday in a raid on homes in the Frankfurt area towns of Langen and Wiesbaden.

But police were still searching for one or more additional suspects in the kidnapping, which has attracted national media attention as the second abduction this year of a well-known German businessman.

A news blackout on the kidnapping was lifted last weekend in hopes of the public helping to find Fiszman, whose family's fortune has been estimated by police to be more than 400 million marks ($260 million).
Fiszman's brother Georg paid a ransom of four million marks on October 10, but his kidnappers reneged on an agreement and failed to free him the following day.
Police said they recovered most of the ransom on Wednesday in the garden of a flat in Wiesbaden owned by Koerppen's parents.
